text: Before you can say a quantum computer is fast at something, you need a precise classical baseline for what fast and hard already mean. This lesson is that baseline, and every later claim in this course about quantum speedup gets measured against it.

P is the class of decision problems a classical computer can solve in polynomial time, like O of n or O of n squared — sorting, primality testing, shortest path all live here. NP is different: it's defined by fast verification, not fast solving. If the answer is yes, there's a certificate a classical computer can check in polynomial time, even if finding that certificate might be hard. NP-complete problems, like SAT, the traveling salesman decision problem, and graph coloring, are the hardest problems in NP — every other NP problem reduces to them, and no polynomial-time algorithm is known for any of them. All of this sits inside the proven chain P is a subset of NP is a subset of PSPACE is a subset of EXPTIME, and whether P equals NP remains one of the most famous open problems in mathematics.

Here's why that chain matters in practice, with real numbers. At n equals 100 — a genuinely small input — O of n is just 100, and O of n squared is 10,000. But O of 2 to the n is 1,267,650,600,228,229,401,496,703,205,376, roughly 1.27 times 10 to the 30th. That's not slow — it's more operations than there are atoms in a small planet. Exponential growth isn't a speed bump, it's a wall.

PSPACE pushes past NP by bounding memory instead of time — a generalized game tree can be explored with only polynomial space, reusing memory as you backtrack, even though the tree has exponentially many nodes. EXPTIME removes the memory restriction entirely and allows time to grow like 2 to the n. Every one of these containments is proven; what's not proven is whether any of them is strict. That unresolved gap, and the exponential wall you just saw, are the exact baseline the rest of this course measures quantum computing against.
Next lesson gives quantum computers their own complexity class, BQP, and asks precisely where it sits against the classical hierarchy you just reviewed.
